utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before the witness is sworn in, the Trial Chamber has a ruling to deliver. The Trial Chamber has noted the submissions of the Prosecution and the Defence response on whether or not any witness requires a warning against self-incrimination. With regard to Defence witness Naser Sejdic, the Prosecution evidence alleges that he participated in some arrests of non-Serbs, notwithstanding the Trial Chamber's ruling under Rule 98 bis, the basis for the said arrests is still a contentious matter. The Defence is entitled to call evidence and their witnesses are entitled to tell their side of events in which -- their side of the events in which they were involved without undue hindrance. The rule on protection against self-incrimination is not absolute. The Trial Chamber can still compel a witness to answer questions even when the answers may lead to self-incrimination. One of the reasons why, in the practice of the Tribunal, the Trial Chamber is allowed to compel witnesses to answer questions in such circumstances is because the Trial Chamber is obliged to receive evidence which is relevant and has probative value in its quest to ascertain the truth. The limited protection for the witness as provided for in Rule 90(E) is sufficient. Otherwise, it would be impossible to obtain evidence on some contentious issues because of limited numbers of eye witnesses in war crime trials such as those before this tribunal. The Trial Chamber is of the view that the solemn declaration taken by every witness in itself is sufficient. Besides, the rule does not require the Trial Chamber to warn the witness ab initio. In this case, the Trial Chamber has no reason to believe that Defence counsel has not fully advised witnesses, especially so when some of the witnesses for the same defendant had applied for safe conduct. The proceedings will continue. And can the witness make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, and if I may say before I start examination of this witness, I would like to assure the Trial Chamber that the witness is fully and properly informed about all his rights and all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Examined by Mr. Lazarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, we have a time limit for your testimony. However, that should not be to the detriment of the clarity of your statement. In order for everything that you say to be recorded properly, could you please pause after answering my question? Pause for a few seconds after my question and then start answering so that the interpreters would have time to interpret what you say. Could you please give your name and surname for the record?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Naser Sejdic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: The 10th of January, 1960 in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married? Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm married and I have two sons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters request that the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The usher can assist. Maybe the witness can also draw closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now, are you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not a member of any political party. I was a member of the League of Communists until the 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, until the 17th of April, 1992, where did you work? Where were you employed and what was your profession?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I completed the school of the interior in Sarajevo in 1980, and it was then, in 1980 that I started to work as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did you work at the police station in Bosanski Samac as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in Bosanski Samac as a policeman. From 1980 onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just going to put one question to you in relation to a particular subject. Were you a member of the 4th Detachment in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No. I was not a member of the 4th Detachment because I worked as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, now I would like to move on to another topic. The 16th of April, 1992, tell me, where were you on that day, what were you doing on that day?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, 1992, I was in my parents' house, together with my wife, and my two sons who were underage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I forgot to put a question to you. Could you please tell me what your ethnic background is?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim, an ethnic Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the 16th of April, 1992, you were in your father's house with your wife and children. Was something unusual going on on that day, the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I did not say one more thing, that my brother was there too as well as my grandmother who was 85 at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice something unusual going on on that particular day, the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: The day was just like the previous few days, everybody was just saying that a war would start.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any particular events occur during the course of that day, something that you might remember, something special related to the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Around 3.00 at night, on the 17th of April, did you hear something perhaps that awakened you? If so, could you please tell the Trial Chamber what it was?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Around 3.00, I heard that there was some shooting in town, shooting from firearms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what did you do? Did you do anything about it? Did you call someone?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. After a while, I called the police station in Bosanski Samac, and nobody answered the phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, that was practically early in the morning, after 3.00, the morning of the 17th. Did you stay at home?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I stayed at home. I didn't go out. I didn't go anywhere. I stayed with my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now we have come to the morning of the 17th of April. Can you tell us what happened in the morning of the 17th of April, sometime, say, after 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: In the morning, around 9.00, a group of some 15 to 20 armed persons came into my street. These were citizens, persons, who I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did they come to your house? Were they in front of your house? I'm sorry, I mean were they in front of your father's house?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were in front of my father's house. They came there and they were carrying Kalashnikovs, hunting guns, pistols, and they called me to come out of the yard and to join them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let us clarify matters regarding this group. First of all, tell me, to the best of your recollection, what were the names of the persons, the armed persons, who came in front of your house and asked to you join them?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I said that these were people from Samac. This was Hasan Bicic, nicknamed Hase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please proceed. You can speak a bit faster?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: His brother, nicknamed Beca. Dagic [as interpreted], Esad, nicknamed Ekac; Ibrahim Salkic, nicknamed Ibela; Dasa; Fadil Sabanovic, nicknamed Suke. There were two brothers, two Sahacic brothers there. Ferhat and the other one, I can't remember the other brother's. Nusret Kapetanovic, nicknamed Saraf. I can't remember any more but there were quite a few there. Dukic, Ciko; Ciko was his nickname. I can't remember -- I remember his last name. I can't remember his first name. I know all the nicknames, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you but for the sake of the transcript, I have been told, when you said Ekac, what is the last name of that person?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Dagovic, Esad Dagovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, since there were a few people with similar nicknames, when you say Dasa --

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Ramusovic, Ramusovic is Dasa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, is he related to you?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is related to me. He is one of my relatives from my mother's side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They called you to join them. What did they tell you, join them in what exactly? Where were they headed for? What were you supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: They called me to join them to go to the memorial centre. It was on that side of Bosanski Samac, that the attack had been carried out, an armed group in camouflage uniforms entered Samac and they said we should go and defend the town of Samac. I asked from whom and they said from some people in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you join the group?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No, I refused to go with them and I told my neighbour, Fadil Sabanovic let's go back to the house. We did not wish to join them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they go eventually?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did. They went towards the memorial centre that was down the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On the 17th of April, did you again try calling the police station?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, about 12.00, and again no one answered the phone. I tried to call the duty officer there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that same day, did you remain at your father's house or in the yard outside the house?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed there with my parents and my family. I didn't leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day, the 18th of April, what happened? What did you experience on the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: About 8.00 in the morning, Ibrahim Salkic arrived outside my father's house. His nickname was Ibela. He told me to get my personal weapons, my official weapons, the weapons that I officially signed for, and to come to the Mola cafe at Rojice [phoen] which is near my father's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did he tell you why you were supposed to take your weapons with you, the weapons you kept at the house?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Yes, yes, he did. That a man named Lugar was expecting me, that those were specials who had arrived from Serbia, who came to collect weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do when Ibrahim Salkic called you?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I collected my Kalashnikov rifle, my official pistol, my hunting weapon, the hunting rifle, and a hunting carbine for which I had a valid permit, and I went towards the cafe. When I arrived in front of the cafe, I saw this man they called Lugar, I didn't know what his name was, but he was sitting on a chair there and everyone else was standing. He asked me what my name was and what I did for life. I told him my name was Naser Sedjic and that I was a police officer because then the force was still referred to as police. At that moment I saw a friend of mine Dragan Miskic, who immediately approached us and he told Lugar something, the man wearing camouflage uniform. I assumed the plan was Lugar and he said where did I get all these weapons and that I should leave it in the car that was parked there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hold on a minute. I believe a part of your answer has not been recorded. Can you tell us who approached Lugar?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: A young man I used to know, his name was Dragan Miskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you didn't hear exactly what he told Lugar?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after he said something to Lugar, please continue. What happened then? Because this was not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Lugar approached another young man and told him to handcuff me and that I should sit down next to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did this man do it? Were you handcuffed?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. He handcuffed me and I sat down next to him. More people were arriving, mostly people from my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, what happened next? Were you taken anywhere?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: After we were handcuffed, we were between ten and 12 people there, they took us down the street and we walked down the street as far as the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what happened once you reached the police station with Lugar?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: There was a young man in camouflage uniform waiting outside the police station, who immediately beat everyone who arrived there. He would beat them and kick them there outside the police station in the street, and our group too, and this man named Dragan came up again and told him not to beat me because we had known each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, where did Lugar take you personally eventually at the police station?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I entered the police station and I reached the duty officer's room, Lugar was following. I looked left and right down the corridor and I noticed on the right-hand side near the duty officer's room my own commander, Savo Cancarevic, who was standing there. Lugar grabbed me by the arm then and took me down the stairs outside to the yard of the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, is this the yard where the garage is? Is that the yard we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, that's the one. Once we were outside in the yard, he pulled out a gun and he asked me how clever I was exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you answer?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I said yes, I should imagine I'm quite clever. So he repeated this several times asking me how clever exactly I was. At that moment, the commander, Savo Cancarevic arrived and Stevan Todorovic, my chief. They told him to let me go, which he did. He called another young man over, they removed my handcuffs, and I went straight to the office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you go to see at the office?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I went to see Savo Cancarevic in his office. I was followed by Chief Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened there?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic then asked whether I wanted to be a Serb policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I agreed. He gave me a beret and a badge. He produced a paper, a document for me to take an oath as a Serb policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that moment, when Stevan Todorovic came up with this proposal, and asked you whether you wanted to be a Serb policeman, what was your impression? Did you really have any choice?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I don't think I had any choice at all. I didn't even have time to think about it because Lugar was standing close to us and Stevan Todorovic and two or three of Lugar's bodyguards wearing camouflage uniforms so I said yes immediately without thinking twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So did you sign this statement, this oath of loyalty, to the Serb police force?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did sign the statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we have shed some light now on the way you became a member of the Serb police on the 18th of April. From the 18th of April on, what did you do, please tell us, as a member of the Serb police, what was your jobs, what were your tasks as a Serb policeman?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: We provided security for buildings. We brought people in to the police station for interviews. We searched people's flats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me about the technical aspects, the purely technical aspects of the job? First you would come to the police station. Can you tell me once you were at the police station, who told you what to do on any particular day, what your daily task would be?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: We were a patrol consisting of five police officers. The leader of the patrol was one of the specials from Serbia. In our patrol it was Zoran, Zoka from Sid. Then he would take the order for that day with -- including the tasks of what we were to do on that particular day, whether we should bring someone in to the police station, whether we should patrol the town or whether we should provide security for a particular building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one thing remaining to be clarified, who was the leader of that patrol?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: As I said, it was a member of the Special Forces from Serbia, who was responsible for us, other members of the patrol, and he told us what to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you personally ever the leader of the patrol?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These tasks you had to carry out, was that something to do with staying at the police station or was it mostly work outside the police building and about the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: We spent very little time at the police station itself. We would only go there for our patrol orders, with specific tasks and we hardly spent any time there at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, can you tell us the following, please? At the SUP building itself, and across the street at the TO building, did you know that there were any persons being held in detention?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did know about people being held there at the SUP building, on the first floor, in three different rooms, on the ground floor in one room and at the TO building across the road from the SUP building, people were even being held in the garages outside in the yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever enter the TO building?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, several times. I would bring food to those people who were being held there because those were my neighbours, people I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your personal observation concerning the people you saw at the TO building? What state were they in?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I didn't have time to linger about for too long but every time I came, they looked as if they had been badly beaten, beaten black and blue. They were totally exhausted and they weren't allowed to talk to me. So the only thing they had is what members of their family sent to them, a sandwich, a piece of food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you directly in a very straightforward way, sir: You personally, did you ever maltreat, beat or verbally abuse any of the prisoners there? Did you torture any of those prisoners there in any other way?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No. I never touched a soul. I never beat anyone. I never tortured anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know that there were people who were detained at the elementary school and the high school in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that there were persons who were detained there as well at the elementary school and the high school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, who guarded these detainees? It's quite clear who guarded them at the police station but what about the elementary school and the high school, who was on guard duty there?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: The police, the police guarded those facilities as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Tell me, to the best of your knowledge, these people who were detained during this first round, so to speak, during the first days of the war, tell me, what was it that you were told, what is it that you learned, why were these people arrested?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: We were told that they were being arrested because they had weapons in their possession, because they were on lists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell me what kind of lists, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: This list was a list of the SDA party, a list of members of the SDA party, and the weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the interests of protecting identity of certain witnesses here we would like to move to private session for some period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, can we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know Jelena Kapetanovic, formerly Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know Jelena Kapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, the patrol that you were on, did it search the apartment where she lived?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. We searched her apartment too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the orders related to her apartment? Do you perhaps remember what were the instructions that you received and why her apartment was to be searched?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: The order said that she had a rifle, a Kalashnikov in her apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did your patrol at one point take Jelena Stanisic to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. We took Jelena to Zasavica. This patrol of ours took Jelena to Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question related to Jelena Kapetanovic, if you remember. At one moment, when one of the exchanges was organised, did you stop Jelena Kapetanovic from boarding the bus that was supposed to take people to the exchange?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I stopped her because she was not on the list for the exchange so I told her that she could not enter the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what were the orders that you had that day in relation to people who were supposed to board the bus and in relation to the list and everything else?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: The order was that these people who were on the list could enter the bus and that we should escort them to Okucani. I think it was Okucani. Okucani, Gradiska, that the police escort with its car was supposed to go to Okucani, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you told about persons who were not on the list?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Whoever was not on the list was not supposed to enter the bus and was supposed to go back to Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Tell me, who gave you these orders? Who gave you orders in the morning generally speaking as to what you were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, we received orders from the duty officer, and these orders and lists were given to the duty officer by Chief Stevan Todorovic, and then we would take them from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, what about the name Hasan Subasic? Does that mean anything to you? Unfortunately I don't know his nickname so I cannot be of any assistance to you in that way.

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Hasan Subasic is a person I cannot remember by his name and surname. I know whose son he is but I really cannot remember him. I cannot remember who this man is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember whether your patrol perhaps took part in the search of his apartment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: How can the witness remember when he says he can't remember this person?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand your witness point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know Kemal Bobic?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know Kemal Bobic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to put a very simple question to you. Did your patrol, the patrol that you were on, arrest Kemal Bobic?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, no. My patrol did not arrest Kemal Bobic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know whether Kemal Bobic was arrested at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects to the evidence my learned friend is leading from this witness in relation to Mr. Bobic. The -- yesterday I filed a notification in relation to witnesses' evidence. Mr. Bobic's evidence was one of the references I included in the notification I filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Under Rule 90(H)(ii) in cross-examination, a party is required to put to a witness evidence which appears to be in contradiction of it given by its -- sorry evidence which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness. Your Honours will know from looking at the transcript of Mr. Bobic's evidence overnight, that the Defence did not in any way challenge Mr. or Mrs. Bobic's account that he was arrested by the patrol containing, including the witness giving evidence here now, and it wasn't something that took the Defence by surprise because it was contained in the statements of both Mrs. Ediba Bobic and Mr. Kemal Bobic which the Defence had had for a long time. And in fact Mr. Pisarevic read to Mr. -- read to Mr. Bobic part of his statement in relation to Mr. Sedjic showing -- what Mr. Sejdic allegedly said that Mr. Lazarevic had allegedly said. So the Prosecution objects to evidence being led to this witness which wasn't put and the Defence had every opportunity to do so, to put its contrary case to the two Bobics at the time. If Your Honours are against me on that, this ultimate submission will be the evidence has no weight at all because of that, because the Bobic's, unless they are recalled have not been given a chance to deny the evidence which is about to be led from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: During all Prosecution case, the Defence of Mr. Zaric denied that Mr. Zaric ordered, that was in position to issue any order to the police officers to arrest anyone. This is nothing that the Prosecution was not aware of and this Trial Chamber was also aware of that. Furthermore, in our summaries, when we proposed this witness, this was the main issue that we wanted this witness to testify about. It is quite obvious that looking through the summaries and our proposal in respect to Rule 71 and testimony of the witnesses, we said that this witness is here to testify about Mr. Zaric allegedly ordered -- ordered him to arrest Kemal Bobic. So I believe that this is not really any ground for this submission of my colleague from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours my objection is specifically under Rule 90(H)(ii). It's not in relation to what the witness -- what Mr. Bobic said that this witness allegedly said about Mr. Zaric. That at its highest, that is hearsay. That Bobic says that Sejdic said that Zaric said something. The Prosecution is stuck with that for the purposes of its case. What I'm objecting to is my learned friend leading evidence from this witness which was not challenged -- not challenged in relation to the two witnesses who gave evidence of this witness arresting Mr. Bobic. The rules are very clear on this. My learned friend -- the rules were clear then. My learned friend's had the statements they are on complete notice of what the evidence was going to be yet did not challenge it. That's my objection. Notwithstanding what -- the one line in the Rule 71 deposition, our notice of what this witness is going to say came at 2 minutes to 9.00 this morning when we received proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is of the view that evidence which is relevant and has probative value and which will assist the Trial Chamber to ascertain the truth will be allowed, notwithstanding the objection of the Prosecution that particular pieces of evidence were not put to the Prosecution witnesses. So the Defence will be allowed to lead evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and if I may add one thing? In the first statement that we were given by the Prosecution of Mr. Kemal Bobic, the statement that he gave to the investigators of the Prosecution, there was no mention of Mr. Zaric. For the first time he mentioned that it was here. We needed of course to check whether this information -- we had instructions of course from our client but we had to do some research in the field but generally we have always one same line of Defence towards arrests and other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I must correct that for the record. The statement of Mr. Bobic which was served on the Defence mentions Mr. Sejdic in two parts and Mr. Zaric in one but in a different part. The issue here is not what Mr. Zaric -- is not what Mr. Zaric said. It's what -- my objection and I'm not cavilling with Your Honour's ruling is in relation to it not being put -- the arrest not being put to the witness, not the part about Mr. Zaric because we don't know what Mr. Zaric said. Only this witness can tell us. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber will not allow technicalities to get in the way of receiving evidence which is relevant. The Defence can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the last question before our exchange with the Prosecution, the patrol that you were on, did you arrest Kemal Bobic? And you said that you didn't. Do you know whether Kemal Bobic was arrested?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do know that he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which patrol precisely arrested, carried out the arrest of Kemal Bobic, who led the patrol that arrested Kemal Bobic?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do know. This policeman known as Sole who arrested him, was on that patrol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did Simo Zaric ever tell you or give you any orders to arrest anyone?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No. Simo Zaric was not the one who gave us orders and he never gave us orders and never told us to do anything. We had our own chief, Stevan Todorovic, who did that, as well as the commander, Savo Cancarevic. So we never had anything to do with Simo Zaric in that respect, in terms of bringing persons in, in terms of searching people's flats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Simo Zaric a member of the police at all? To the best of your knowledge, of course.

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm telling you. He was not a member of the police. We had our own commanding officers, our own superiors, in the police. Simo Zaric had nothing whatsoever to do with the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll just ask you another question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, your time has been up --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm afraid I didn't pay much attention. There was some exchange of arguments between the Prosecution, there is literally two more minutes to complete this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please wind up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, as a member of the police, did you ever take part in any actions together with the army?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did take part in operations together with the army. Joint operations with the army, rather, as a police officer. We went to Gorice, to the front line in Gorice together with the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when were you led to that operation, as a police officer, who was the leader of the police in that operation?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: We went there with the Special Forces from Serbia where we had -- who had their own commander, Lugar, and the army was in charge of the operation. The command was based in Pelagicevo for that operation. [Realtime transcript read in error "A."] The commander was Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one last thing, after the end of this operation --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we please clarify when that was?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the benefit of my colleague from the Prosecution, please tell us the time frame?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I think it was in May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once the operation was completed, what happened to you? Did you go back to your usual job as policeman?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as the operation was completed, we returned to Samac, and we went back to our old jobs, the jobs that we had been doing before, as police officers. We never had anything else to do with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much Mr. Sejdic. I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, does anybody from the Defence wish to ask questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, first of all, just intervention to the transcript, it's at page 22, line 16 until 19, in line 19, the answer should be added to the previous answer, because it is not so clear. Because we have two answers. First sentence starts with word we went there, et cetera, et cetera, and then after the word operation, should be added the -- just for the sake of clarity of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That will be corrected because it's part of -- it's a continuous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, my name is Pantelic. I defend Mr. Blagoje Simic before there Tribunal. Just a couple of issues. You were born in Samac. You worked there. For the whole duration of the war and even nowadays, do you still reside in Samac?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was born in Samac. I spent the whole war in Samac. I still reside in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As concerns your family, were they also in Samac for the whole time with you? Are they still there?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, my family too. We all live there together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the war, did you reside in your flat, you and your family? Please explain to the Trial Chamber what was the situation concerning where you lived. Did anyone expel you from any of your flats or did you stay there for the whole time?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I resided in my flat. My parents and my brother have their own family house. That's where they were. No one drove us out of the flat or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Sejdic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, thank you we have several questions for this witness. Cross-examined by Mr. Krgovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sejdic, my name is Dragan Krgovic, I will ask you a number of questions on behalf of Mr. Miroslav Tadic's defence. My learned colleague, Lazarevic asked you questions in relation to orders for bringing persons in which you were receiving from your superiors, Todorovic and Cancarevic. Tell me, please, and obviously you received your orders through your patrol leader. Is that what you told my colleague, Lazarevic? I mean the chain was let me explain this, it was Chief of Police or the commander, the duty officer, the patrol leader, and then the order would finally reach you? Is that how it happened?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Precisely. That's how we obtained our lists [as interpreted]. The duty officer would give it to the patrol leader. Sometimes he would read the order, sometimes I would read it but it came from the duty officer, from the chief of the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This order would contain the name of the person to be brought in for an interview and the reasons for it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what it contained, first and last name of the person, and the reason for the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you but page 25, line 1, the witness answered the question, "Yes, yes, precisely, that's how we obtained our lists." Is that the correct word or should it be orders? Is he now talking about orders in connection with exchanges or performing other duties? Because this sounds a bit strange, to talk about lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It's probably a misinterpretation. I'm asking the witness about the circumstances surrounding the bringing in of persons to the police station for interviews. And what he said instead of list, we should have order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, the transcript says list. What you mean is an order to bring someone in to be interviewed with the names of persons and the reasons for the interview. Just please say it loud and clear into the microphone for the sake of the transcript. You nodded.

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, this was a written order, was it? Or was it an oral order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a written order. Patrol order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, this procedure of bringing persons into the police station, was this done the same way even before the war in Bosanski Samac? Was the procedure the same?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, the procedure was the same before the war and during the war. We would receive orders to bring someone in for an interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, would you do anything outside that order or would you adhere strictly to orders issued according to standard police procedure?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: We followed the orders strictly, the orders as issued to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Sejdic. I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution? Cross-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, my name is David Re, I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution. The first question I wish to ask you is in relation to your own arrest by Lugar, I think you said it was on the 18th or 19th of April, 1992. When you were arrested, no reason was given for your arrest, was it?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: It happened on the 18th of April. They were arresting everyone in my neighbourhood. As I said, between ten and 12 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please listen to the question I asked. My question was no one gave you any reason for your arrest, did they?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No. No one gave me any reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people in your neighbourhood, were they Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only reason you know that you and those other people were arrested was because they were Muslims, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object. First of all, my -- first of all, my dear colleague asked the witness whether he was given any reason and he said not any reason was given to him why he was arrested and now he is giving some reason for him and asking him to speculate. If he doesn't know the reason, how could he know why he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, the question is proper for the Prosecution. They are suggesting to him so the witness should be able to answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only reason you and the other people, the other Muslims were arrested was because they were Muslims, right?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: That's not correct, that that was the reason. We all carried our weapons, my neighbours too, and we took it into the car when we arrived outside the cafe, and that was the reason why we were arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, after the paramilitaries seized control of Bosanski Samac municipality on the night of the 17th of April, 1992, they started arresting large numbers of Muslims and Croats, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that process continued over a period of months, didn't it? Arrests of Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Only those who had weapons and those whose names were on lists were arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that old women and children's names are on lists of people who should have been arrested, sir? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we have no evidence about arrested children and -- here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is my learned friend suggesting that taking people to isolation facilities isn't arresting them or detaining them unlawfully? Is that what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, maybe there can be a problem with technicalities there. We have been using the word isolation generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please the Tribunal. I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence sir is that the only people who were arrested in Bosanski Samac after the 17th of April, 1992, in that year, who were Muslims and Croats, were people on lists allegedly suspected of arming? Is that your evidence before this Trial Chamber, sir?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question. Can you try to put a more concise question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hundreds of Croats and Muslims were arrested in Bosanski Samac after the 17th of April, 1992 by Serbian police and regular police, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just intervention. We heard in B/C/S language something which may be confused for this witness, in last question of my learned friend. I know that in English, it sounds proper, Serbian police and regular police, but what we heard in B/C/S language, as well as this witness, is that it was not related to the Serbian police from Serbia and regular police from Samac. It sounds that it is the same category in two words. So maybe that could be corrected. Maybe my learned friend just can rephrase the question when saying police who came -- which came from Serbia or specials or volunteers or whatever, and a local police, in order to clarify that, because in B/C/S language we heard practically two words with the same notion, which is confusing. That was the basis of my intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just note that that objection or intervention took one minute of my -- and seven seconds of the cross-examination. I can clarify a question but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But I think it's fair to the witness if you are more particular when you are talking about the police because as Mr. Pantelic does say, and he -- and even the witness was talking about Lugar so I think it's better to be precise as to which group you're referring to when you're talking about the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will do that but the trouble is Your Honour with cross-examination limits instead of asking the four questions to get to that, I'm trying to role it up into one and paraphrase it. That's the difficulty with this. So I'll go back and try and do it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, my question was after the 17th of April, 1992, police arrested hundreds of Croats and Muslims in Bosanski Samac, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: The special police force from Serbia, they were the ones who were arresting people. I did say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, your own evidence earlier was that you participated in patrols that went around arresting people. Are you saying that you were a member of these special police when you were doing that?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No. The special police were arresting people. One of them was with us, this man named Zoran. He was in our patrol. We were to bring people in for interviews, not to arrest them, people from the town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people whose houses you went to with this member of the special police in company with other police officers from Bosanski Samac, those people whose houses you went to didn't have a choice about whether they went with you or stayed behind, did they?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: They did have a choice. They did not have to go with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: We brought the people whose -- we did not bring everyone whose houses we had entered. We did not bring anyone to the police station. It was only if we found weapons in a certain flat, say, then the person who owns the flat would be taken in for an interview. Many people did not need to come with us to the police station to be interviewed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your evidence to this Trial Chamber that you personally, in company with the other police and the Serb police or paramilitaries or whoever, never arrested and took to the police station a single person in whose house you didn't find weapons? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No, no. That's not my evidence. Those whose names were not included in the order, because there were names of people that were included in the order to be taken in for an interview, and they didn't have weapons, and they were released immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please concentrate on what I'm asking you. I'm asking you this: Are you saying that you and the other Serb police officers from wherever never arrested a single person, that is took them to the police station, involuntarily or under arrest, unless they had weapons? Did you only take people to the police station who had no choice other than to come with you who had weapons? That's what I'm asking you. That you had found weapons in the house. That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I must apologise. I don't want to interrupt my colleague but this question, there are at least four to five versions of what he is putting to the witness. Could he please ask the witness simple, short questions? I really couldn't follow even myself what was the question of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This witness has answered. If you look at the answer on page 30, line 24, he has explained that those whose names were not included in the order, because there were names of people that were included in the order to be taken in for an interview and they didn't have weapons and they were released immediately. So there were two categories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware, your evidence has been to this effect, that prisoners held at the SUP, the MUP and the two schools -- sorry, the SUP, the TO and the two schools were treated abominably by those detaining them?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were being beaten. I saw that myself. They were in prison at the police station, the TO building too, whenever I went there. I said that I saw people there who had been beaten by the specials, by the special police, and I did say that. Because they were the ones who brought them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That included people whose names were on the lists and people whose names were not on lists, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: This included people whose names were on the lists and those people who had been imprisoned because they were in possession of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the 17th of April onwards in Bosanski Samac, whoever was responsible for this had established a system in which prisoners were systematically beaten and tortured in detention facilities, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No, no, not systematically tortured. Those specials, you know, they would get drunk, they would go to the TO building, and beat those people there but it was no systematic torture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is clear evidence before this Tribunal, this Trial Chamber, Mr. Sejdic, of Mr. Todorovic who has admitted himself beating torturing and even killing prisoners in the police station. He was in charge of the police station. I'm suggesting to you he put in place a system in that police station which was of systematic brutality to those who were held. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree just like that. They did beat them. He did beat them and the specials beat them too but I never personally witnessed any beatings. When those people, those detainees, were being beaten. I knew that he was there and I knew that the specials were beating them but if on a systematic scale, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You worked in that police station from the 17th of April, after the change of -- after the takeover right through that year, didn't you? On a full-time basis.

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, from the 17th of April on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Everyone who was working in that police station was aware that prisoners were being beaten and tortured regularly, weren't they, including yourself?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: We did hear about that, yes, people being beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that happened and you knew about that from the first few days after the 17th of April, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I knew about that. I knew about people being beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew that Todorovic was responsible for some of the beatings, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew that prisoners who or people who were being asked to come to the police station for questioning were at risk of being beaten by the specials coming in and Todorovic and other people, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: The people I brought over to the police station, I would just hand them over to the duty officer. Now what happened to them later, there was no way for me to know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not a serious answer, sir, is it?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you, I would bring persons over to the police station, and we would hand these persons over to the duty officer and we had nothing more to do with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew the system of interrogations taking place in that police station after the 17th of April, 1992, was very, very different from the procedures which you had experienced before the war, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's true that I knew the system was different now. But this was not my decision, whether someone would be beaten or not. I had to bring those people in, if I can clarify to you this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout that year, you brought in people to the police station knowing that they were at risk of being beaten senseless by Stevan Todorovic, his men or specials from Serbia, didn't you? Because you knew that was happening in the police station.

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: We didn't keep bringing them in for the whole year. I'm talking about my patrol. I'm talking about myself. We brought people in and kept doing so for the first ten or 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's 10.31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will take our break and continue at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. I thought I had asked to you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is nothing on the transcript. I didn't hear anything. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, at the time you were working in the police station in 1992, there were no Serbs in custody being beaten by Todorovic and the other Serb paramilitaries -- or the Serb paramilitary or police, were there?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No. There were two Serbs who were detained, who were also beaten, and after a few days, they were released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from those two, all the other people who were being -- who were arrested and detained in that SUP, the TO, the elementary school and the primary school were all Muslims and Croats, the people who were being beaten, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All of them were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was obvious to you and everyone else working for the police, working from that SUP, that Croats and Muslims were being arrested because they were Croats and Muslims, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object. This is the second time my colleague is posing the same question and the witness already gave the answer what was his knowledge as what was the reason for the arrest of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No that was in relation to his own arrest and the arrest of the people in his neighbourhood on the 17th of April. I'm now asking him about the people he has just described as being in detention in the SUP, the TO and the two schools after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you understand my question, those Croats and Muslims who I've just spoken about who were in the SUP, the TO and the two schools, were there were arrested because they were Muslims and Croats, correct?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were arrested because they were Muslims and Croats, who had weapons at their houses. I already said that. And this was on the lists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any members of the clergy, without mentioning names, on the list who had possession of weapons? No names, please, but just members of the clergy?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: There was a member of the clergy who did not have any weapons and who was there nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was tortured and beaten while in custody by the Serbs, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only reason you know of for his arrest was because he was a Croat, correct?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Because he was a clergyman?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because he was a Croat, sir.

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: All right. A Croatian clergyman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Serbs were not being arrested for possession of weapons or having their name on lists, were they?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Serbs were not being arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The system of arrest was directed solely at Muslims and Croats, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The system of interrogation of those who were arrested, that is the Muslims and Croats, was directed solely at Muslims and Croats, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I'm just telling you, it was directed solely at those who had weapons, those were the ones who were being interrogated. Serbs -- no, sorry, Croats and Muslims who were on lists, they were brought in for interviews and they were interrogated in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we've already established there was a member of the clergy, a Croat member of the clergy who wasn't on those lists but was nevertheless interrogated and brought in. What I'm asking you about is the system there which was directed solely at Muslims and Croats. Everyone working in the police station knew and everyone taking part in the arrests, the interrogations, knew that it was directed solely at Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't answer. Objection, Your Honours. The witness has already answered several times that he knew that these Muslims and Croats were arrested and interrogated because of weapons, and now again he's being asked to speculate whether that was the kind of system that had been established. He said that he knew about his reasons -- about the reasons why these people were being arrested and interrogated. And it is speculation to ask whether everybody at the police station knew about that. How can he know what everybody thought and knew?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The witness was working there, during the crucial period he can certainly give his evidence as to his knowledge of the knowledge of the other people participating in the system and that is what I am asking him about. If he doesn't know, he can tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And I think you have spent a lot of time on this point. Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm asking you is this system which you agreed was in place of arresting Muslims and Croats, Serbs were not being arrested for possession of weapons, that means it was a discriminatory system against Croats and Muslims because Serbs were also in possession of weapons, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll start again. As a police officer in Bosanski Samac in 1992 you were aware that Serbs were also arming as well as the SDA and HDZ, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: None of those Serbs who were arming themselves were arrested and detained in any of the four detention centres I have mentioned for illegal possession of weapons or arming, were they?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Why would they be arrested? What would the reason be for that? Would the grounds be illegal possession of weapons? Is that what you mean? What would the reason be?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, sir --

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Serbs, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said Serbs. Are you suggesting that the SDS arming itself or Serbs arming themselves were somehow in a different category in terms of the law and illegal arming to Croats, Muslims, members of the SDA and HDZ? Is that what you're saying, Serbs are in their own category?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Answer my question, then. My question was the fact that the Serbs were not being arrested but the other two groups were meant that they were discriminatory arrests, correct? He was doing the arresting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I know he was. He was a member of patrol who brought people into SUP, and to be fair to the witness, the decision about who will be arrested eventually when one is brought in the SUP was not up to him or other members -- maybe other members of patrol. Asking him about legal position of Serbs who were not being brought in the SUP or whether they were not, and asking him to speculate whether there was any system of why these arrests were -- he is a factual witness and he cannot be a legal expert to give any kind of explanation whether there was a system or -- of persecution or something like that. He very simply answered that he's aware that most -- a great majority of people who were arrested were Croats and Muslims and asking him to drive one line or system or something like that, I really don't believe it's fair to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber doesn't see anything wrong with the question of the witness, because this witness did get involved in these arrests and he was -- and he was in Bosanski Samac for that whole period so he should be able to know whether or not the system was discriminatory. He can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is simply this: The fact that the Serbs were not being arrested for doing what the Croats and Muslims were doing, that is arming themselves from what you saw meant that those arrests of non-Serbs was discriminatory. The arrests were made on discriminatory grounds, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Serbs were not being arrested, only Croats and Muslims who had weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Likewise, the interrogations in the police station of those people who had been arrested on discriminatory grounds were likewise discriminatory because Serbs were not being interrogated for the same alleged crimes that Muslims and Croats were. Those interrogations were just as discriminatory, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer to my question about the interrogations following the arrests of Muslims and Croats being just as discriminatory as the reasons for their arrest? You agree with me, don't you, that the interrogations were just as discriminatory as the reasons for arresting only Muslims and Croats, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I don't know what they interrogated them about. That's the problem. That's why I can't answer your question. How do I know what they asked them once we brought them in. Once we brought them into the station. I did not bring Serbs into the station. I only brought in Muslims and Croats. How can I know what they talked about to them and what they asked them about? Is this a clear answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the fact of their interrogation. The fact that they were interrogated in the station as you knew that they were, was a discriminatory basis for interrogating them, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours. The witness clearly and decidedly said that he did not know what they talked about and what they talked about. He said that he did not bring in Serbs, that he brought in only Muslims and Croats, and he cannot make any distinction between the reasons why Serbs were not being arrested and the reasons why Muslims and Croats were being arrested. After all, the conflict in Bosanski Samac was between the Muslims and Croats on one side and the Serbs on the other side. So they were arresting the enemy, people who were on the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you are not a witness. So that will not be taken into account. The witness can answer the question being put by Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You understand the question? It is based only on the fact that they were interrogated, not what was said because you said you weren't there. The fact that non-Serbs were interrogated after their arrest which you have agreed was on discriminatory grounds because they were non-Serbs, the fact of their interrogation itself was discriminatory too, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, they interrogated only Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were aware in that time you were working in the police station that a terrible system was in place in Bosanski Samac against the non-Serbs, that is of arresting them, detaining them, and beating them. It was a terrible system in place, sir, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was a system or not. I told you at the very outset why they were being arrested and what was going on. I said that. It's not that this was something systematic that was being done. As I said to you from the very beginning, people were being brought in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back a step. You were a police officer who you say was forced to change sides and start working for the Serbs. You've agreed with that. The Serbs had taken control of the town, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Serb military and civilian authorities were in control of Bosanski Samac after the 17th of April, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These military -- these military and civilian authorities were the JNA in the 4th Detachment, the paramilitaries, and the Crisis Staff, correct?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Samac, as you had put it, was taken by the Serbian police. The Serbian police in particular. And the 4th Detachment on the other hand, there was no army there at the beginning at all. The army had not come in yet. There was only the 4th Detachment and the special police from Serbia. They were the ones who took Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic was your Chief of Police and you were taking orders from him, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the Chief of Police, Stevan Todorovic. But there was a special police from Serbia there that took Samac, and I got my orders from Stevan Todorovic, Chief of Police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went with these special police to people's houses to ask them to come to the police station or to answer some questions and you went with -- I'm sorry, when you went to these people's houses you said it was on Todorovic's orders. Todorovic ordered you and the special police to do this, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Todorovic ordered our police patrol, gave orders to our police patrol, and this police patrol was headed by a member of the special police force, and when he saw people, he introduced himself as a member of the special police force that came in from Serbia, that is how he introduced himself and then he would tell people that on the orders of Stevan Todorovic, they were supposed to be brought in. I don't know if I'm being clear. Our patrol consisted of five people, a member of the special police force from Serbia headed the patrol. Then we would take an order from the duty officer, an order issued by Stevan Todorovic, as to whose house we should go to, whose house we should search and who we should bring in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was giving orders to the member of the special -- to the Serbian special person who headed these patrols, sir?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Who gave him orders? The duty officer at the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The duty officer who was under Todorovic was giving the whole patrol, that is the Serbian special paramilitary police officer and the members of the Bosanski Samac police, is that what you're saying, all the orders came from Todorovic to the duty officer to all of those on the patrol?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serbian police officers or the special paramilitaries or whatever you call them, are you saying they were under Todorovic's control, when they worked from the police station?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: The leader of the patrol was under the control of Todorovic, and he went with us -- I mean, he was under Todorovic's orders. Not under his control. The special police did have its own commander but he acted on Todorovic's orders only when he would go out on patrol with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know Dr. Blagoje Simic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you known him for?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I know him, he's from Samac. I mean, I've known him all the time. I mean we are the same generation, from Samac. I mean I've known him for as long as he's been in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that he's a friend of mine. He's an acquaintance. We know each other but we did not socialise. He's not a friend of mine, although we've known each other for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware during the war that he was the President of the Crisis Staff and War Presidency, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him at the SUP when you were working there and if so, how many times?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see him at the SUP. I never saw him at the SUP. I saw him in town a few times, in passing, but it's not that I saw him coming to the SUP, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Miroslav Tadic? You know him too, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know Tadic too. He's from Samac too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were working at the police station in 1992, did you and if so how many times did you see Mr. Tadic there?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I never saw him at the police station but I did see him in town often. I often saw him in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw him on exchanges too, didn't you, Mr. Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him once during an exchange. He was walking around the school yard where the exchange was supposed to start.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your role in that exchange, Mr. Sejdic, and when was it?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, that exchange was -- I mean it involved about ten [Realtime transcript read in error "Q."] detainees. One bus or two buses of civilians were going to be exchanged in Croatia in order to reunited with their families. So I was actually escorting that exchange. I mean there had to be a police escort. For their own safety we were supposed to take them to Okucani. I think that's where the exchange was to take place, yes n Okucani, and I read the list, who could board the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the record, it was recorded the answer that the witness gave as a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, it will be corrected. It continues. It is about ten detainees, one bus --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us when that exchange was, to the best of your memory, please?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the month when that exchange took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you attended the exchange in the capacity of escorting people to the exchange place. You were doing that as a police officer, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who ordered you to accompany the people on the exchange?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
