utterances.text: From the police station. The Chief of Police provided a list and we took the list from the duty officer. We got this patrol order to go and escort these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many other exchanges did you and the other police working from the police station participate in, in your official capacity?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I was in two exchanges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on each occasion, were you ordered to do so by the duty officer who had got his orders from Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric has given a statement to this -- to the Office of the Prosecutor which is in evidence here, sir, in which he says between the 17th of April, 1992, and the 1st of May, 1992, and that is Exhibit P141, page 5 of the English, where he said, "Now I was going to the SUP for about two or three hours a day, the rest of the time I was in the field and visiting units and carrying out tasks, that I had to do. During that time when I went there --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down? The reading is too fast to follow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "During that time when I went there it was to conduct, and this is what I did, interviews with the following people and I did," and he then names people. That's between the 17th of April and the 1st of May, 1992. Zaric said he was going there two or three hours a day. How many times did you see Mr. Zaric from memory -- how many times did you see Mr. Zaric at the SUP - just let me finish - in that period?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: In that period, I saw him two or three times. I saw him come to the police station, two or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your -- the police went to the front line with the JNA at one point. Was it the JNA or the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: It was the Army of Republika Srpska. With its command in Pelagicevo. Oh, no. No. It was the JNA. Can I correct this? Can I make a correction? This is right. It was the JNA that was there. Their tank was there up at Gorice. Before the Army of Republika Srpska was established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following the takeover on the -- about the 19th of April, you as a police officer, were guarding the waterworks with members of the JNA, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: We, the police, guarded the waterworks and the post office. It was only the police that was guarding these facilities, not members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your evidence in chief to Mr. Lazarevic, you spoke -- you told us and you've agreed with me that you knew about the prisoners being detained in the two schools. You performed guard duties at those schools, didn't you, Mr. Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Once I was on guard duty by the gym in the elementary school but throughout this period I was there only once when I was there on guard duty, nobody came to the detainees who were there at the school and nobody beat them, nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to know, Mr. Sejdic, is who ordered you to go and perform guard duty that night or that day.

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: For providing security for the school the waterworks or any facility, there was a schedule that was made by the assistant commander, I think, that was his post, Milan Jekic. He was the person who said who would go to perform guard duties. He was in charge of making the schedule as to who would go to which facility for guard duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which authorities were controlling the schools, the detention facilities in the schools? Who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Which authorities you mean? The police, the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the police, do you mean the Serb police commanded by Stevan Todorovic and including the paramilitaries? Are they the police you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: The police whose chief was Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the paramilitaries also, that is the specials, from Serbia, were they also helping to control the school, the detainees in the schools?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, they were there, they did not assist. They were not helping. I mean we were the ones who were guarding the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the paramilitaries or the Serbian specials doing when you were there guarding -- when you, that is the police, were guarding the schools?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one small intervention in the transcript on page 49, line 6, the witness actually answered they were together with us in the same building, meaning the SUP building. This part of the answer was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: M'hm. Yes, perhaps the witness can be asked to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic what I'm asking you is I want to know, I want the Trial Chamber to know, who was guarding the detention facilities, the two schools, the SUP and the TO. You've said the police were there on a roster or a schedule. I want to know about the involvement of the people from Serbia, the special police or paramilitaries or whatever you call them. What was their involvement in guarding or controlling these four facilities, as briefly, as you can, please.

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: The police provided security there. The police. The Serb police. That is to say that this special police, if I can call it that, could enter whenever they wanted to. Although we guards were there, that is the kind of powers they had. It's not powers. They could walk in whenever they wanted to, into any room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were guarding these facilities, did you let the Serb special police in?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We already have the answer to that. A minute ago. When he was asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And furthermore, I would like to know whether some frames -- timeframes are also applied to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Because it's been more than 45 minutes that they are posing questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just say --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just say this? For the Prosecution point this is the first witness -- almost in the category of an insider witness, to come here to give evidence of -- besides Todorovic whose evidence really needs corroboration to give evidence of inside workings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. There are no rules on corroboration in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But in terms of the final submission he is the first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, wind up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will wind up, I don't need much longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Just winds up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, these arrests or visits to people's houses to ask them to come to the police station continued throughout 1992, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No. This -- in 1992 but I don't know until when, for the first ten or 15 days. It lasted until May or thereabouts, late April, early May, the first 20 days. That's the police did those searches for the first ten or 15 days in the town of Samac, when we brought persons in like I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about not just the searches but taking people to the police station for interrogation. That continued throughout 1992 against Muslims and Croats, didn't it? It didn't end after the first ten to 15 days, did it?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: What I'm telling you is that I worked for ten or 15 days on those jobs. Now as for later, when they were brought in and how many of them were brought in, I really don't know because I was no longer on the same job.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew that people were being isolated in Zasavica on the orders of Todorovic, that is Croats and Muslims, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that people were being taken there against their will to be isolated, kept separate from the community. You knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that they were taking them there on the chief's orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please don't answer that. This is the problem I alerted Your Honours to yesterday in relation to the witness's evidence, with that knowledge what he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you have to wind up. The Trial Chamber is very much aware of the answers the witness is giving.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The difficulty is what's on the transcript and the protection for the witness, Your Honour. That's why I specifically raised that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can you just wind up? The Trial Chamber is very much aware of your concerns, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If the Court pleases. I have nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Re-examination Mr. Lazarevic? Re-examined by Mr. Lazarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us just briefly dwell on a number of answers that you gave to my colleague from the Prosecution. In connection with a certain system, which the Prosecutor referred to during cross-examination, they put it to you that there was a system according to which people were beaten, tortured and arrested. Are you aware of the existence of any system at all there?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of the existence of any system. When they said systematically, I don't know that people were systematically beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's precisely what I want to learn about. What do you know about the beatings of people and the torture of people? Did they unfold according to a certain pattern, a system, or was it really down to personal decisions taken by individual police officers or specials or Stevan Todorovic to beat any of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, every time they got drunk, they walk about town, nab someone and beat them and the same thing happened at the police station. They beat whoever they liked and whenever they liked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we've dwelt for long enough on this topic. While putting their case to you, as they said, the Prosecutor suggested that the people who were being brought into the SUP building for questioning had been beaten before they were interviewed. That's their chronology. Do you know this for a fact or rather do you know anything about that, about people being beaten, whatever you know about people being beaten? You've already answered but was that to the best of your knowledge related to any further statements that were made?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I said they beat whoever they liked. That's why there was -- before the statement and after the statement and they beat whoever they brought in and they beat up the two Serbs who had been detained as well. And a number of other people too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked by the Prosecutor a number of questions related to the Serbs arming themselves prior to the conflict. And among other things, you referred to the 4th Detachment in your answer. The 4th Detachment, was it armed by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do know that it was armed by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In or about January or February, 1992, the JNA was the army of Yugoslavia, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina was part of Yugoslavia then, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the weapons that people from the 4th Detachment obtained had been provided by the regular army of an existing state; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far, in this trial, we have had evidence that there were quite a number of Muslims who were members of the 4th Detachment also. Were they too given weapons by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do object now. My questions were directed at the parties arming themselves. I didn't ask about the JNA or the 4th Detachment arming itself. It seems to be going way beyond cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it was the Serbs arm themselves. It wasn't a question of whether SDS armed their members. The question was did Serbs arm themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, some of the time, yes, you simply said Serbs Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But any way I won't elaborate this topic any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague from the Prosecution asked you about -- my apologies. I still don't have your answer to my previous question. It has not been recorded. Were there Muslims too who were given weapons as members of the 4th Detachment by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were quite a number of Muslims there too, fewer Croats but there were both Muslims and Croats who were in the 4th Detachment who were given weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Prosecutor asked you questions about the statements and people being interviewed at the police station. I know because you told us that you were not present there yourself, and that you are not aware of the contents of those statements given by those who were interviewed. What I want to know is who was at the police station, who took the statements from those persons, who were the police inspectors initially?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: The police inspectors at that time were Rados Sarkanovic, his boss was Milos Simic, the two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said Milos Simic. I think the last name was Savic, actually?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Milos Savic, that's who I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you perhaps know that the specials, members of the Special Forces from Serbia, as you called them, also sometimes interviewed persons of their own initiative?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Re asked you about seeing Mr. Zaric at the police station and your answer was that you saw him perhaps three times during that period, if I remember correctly, first of all let me ask you: You've told us already but did you spend most of your time at the station or rather elsewhere in the field?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I spent most of my time outside in the field. I would only come to the station briefly and I only saw Simo in passing, perhaps two or three times like I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the two or three times you did see Simo Zaric, what sort of uniform was he wearing? Police or military? That's my question. It's a simple one too.

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I've understood your question. He was wearing camouflage, military uniform

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In one of your answers to the Prosecutor, you referred to the 4th Detachment in Bosanski Samac. Can you please just confirm the following, namely that the 4th Detachment was deployed along the embankment in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can confirm that. Along the embankment facing the River Bosna, from the side of Prud.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally see this?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did, personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That wasn't raised in cross-examination, anything about the embankment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware that it wasn't. It wasn't raised by the -- in questions of my learned colleague but it was raised by the witness in his answer but any way, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise for this. There was one question I forgot to ask which I should have put to the witness under Rule 90(H) in relation to the Prosecution's case of Mr. Bobic. Could I have leave to put this one question to him and of course Mr. Lazarevic could answer anything -- I anticipate it's going to be a very short answer. I just have to put a proposition to the witness while he's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic I just have one question and that is, I want to suggest to you that on or about the 17th of April, 1992, Mr. Bobic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you give the full name, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Kemal Bobic was told by Bosanski Samac police that he had to report to the police station twice a day and not leave the house. He had to report twice a day either by phone or in person. I want to suggest that he asked you who had ordered this and you told him that it was Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: No. No. I did not talk to Bobic about that at all. I don't even know that he had to report twice every day to the police. He probably reported to the duty officers, not to us, the police officers, who were patrolling the town. He would go to the duty officer. I was not in touch with him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours for your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no redirect on this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, there wouldn't be any, I think. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I just have two questions to ask. On line -- page 21, lines 19 to 21, Mr. Sejdic, you are responding to a question posed by Mr. Lazarevic, and this also concerned the arrest of Mr. Kemal Bobic, and in connection with that, you say, "So we never had anything to do with Simo Zaric in that respect, in terms of bringing persons in, in terms of searching people's flats." So my question is: In what respect did you have something to do with Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: In terms of giving orders, if he'd had the -- he did not have the authority -- can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. You were asked by Mr. Lazarevic, this is page 22, line 14, Mr. Lazarevic says to you, "Did Simo Zaric ever tell you or give you any orders to arrest anyone?" And then your answer is, "No, Simo Zaric was not the one who gave us orders and he never gave us orders and never told us to do anything." And then I'll miss out the next line to do with Mr. Todorovic. And then you go on to say, "So we never had anything to do with Simo Zaric in that respect, in terms of bringing persons in, in terms of searching people's flats." Now, I'm interested in those three words, "In that respect." The implication is there were other matters, other than bringing persons in and searching people's flats, that you did have an involvement with Mr. Zaric. And I would just like you to explain what that was.

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: When I said that we didn't -- that we never had anything with Simo Zaric, I meant that he was never our commander. We had our own command, the police. Our own chief who gave us orders, Savo Cancarevic. It was in that sense that I said that we never had anything to do with Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So you never had anything to do with Simo Zaric at all? Am I understanding you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely. Nothing to do whatsoever with Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And my second question relates to answers to a question posed by Mr. Lazarevic on page 30, lines -- well, line 13 actually. You were being asked as to the collection of -- well, going to people's houses, and you were asked whether persons had a choice about whether they went with you or stayed behind. And your answer on line 13 is, "They did have a choice. They did not have to go with us." So Mr. Sejdic, my question to you is: If somebody said, "I don't want to go with you," what would have happened to him or her? Did you have orders in that respect if somebody said, "No, I don't want to go to the SUP"?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: There was no need for the person to follow us back to the SUP. The person didn't have to. We wouldn't force the person to go. But if we found a Kalashnikov in the person's flat or any other weapon, he had to follow us back to the station. Then he was not in a position to refuse. There would be -- we would take other steps, we would bring the person in to the police station, so that was not something a person could refuse if a weapon was found in the person's flat. If there was nothing, for example, then the person was free to say there is no need for me to go. In fact we would never ask such a person to go. That's what I tried to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sejdic, I have a couple of questions. You told us that your patrol searched the flat of Jelena Kapetanovic. Did that happen once or twice?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Only once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Only once. Okay. Do you remember the persons present during that search of her flat? Were there, for instance, any members of the 4th Detachment present at that time?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: When we searched flats, there were no members around. It was our police patrol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Well, then you told us that you had a Kalashnikov in your possession. Was that the personal weapon of all policemen?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, personal weapon, my own. My own personal weapon, yes, all policemen had Kalashnikovs as personal weapons, officially issued weapons. And a pistol, too, a hand gun. And a truncheon too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: You didn't go to the police station on the 16th, nor on the 17th of April. Were you off duty or what was the reason that you didn't go to the -- your place of work?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: On the 16th and on the 17th, I had days off. On the 18th I was supposed to start work at 6.00 in the morning and that's why I called on the phone on the 16th in the morning. I called the duty officer and on the 17th too I just wanted to know whether I would be required to go to work or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just to follow up with one short question, Mr. Sejdic, following from Judge Lindholm's question as to the visit to the apartment of Mrs. Jelena Kapetanovic, do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Would you recall whether it was after she had been brought back from a period of detention or isolation in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, but first we carried out the search and then after that, she was taken into isolation. Before the search. But when she came back from detention, I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I was talking about her stay in Crkvina, not her isolation in Zasavica. Does that -- do you have any knowledge about Crkvina and whether this visit by yourself and your patrol was before or after that?

utterances.speaker: NASER SEJDIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about Crkvina or when she was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for giving evidence. We are through now. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Re please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry, I'll start again. While the witness is coming in may I tender into evidence a portion of Kemal Bobic's statement only on the issue of credibility of the last witness, which Mr. Pisarevic got from Mr. Bobic as being a true and correct statement? That was the matter I put to the witness at the very end, and it's only a portion of a statement dated the 3rd of April, 1998, between the Prosecutor and Kemal Bobic. One paragraph of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object. I object to this. First of all, if Mr. Re had some document to put before this witness, he shouldn't have waited for the witness to leave and then try to put it on the back door here in evidence. Just to show him, to say this is this and give him to read that and give his comment. And then if -- and then he should have asked for admission of this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I did both. I read to him the extract and now I'm asking to put it into evidence. I didn't do it while the witness was here because I wanted to do it while someone else was being brought in which I thought it was the most appropriate time to save time. It's no secret. It's a document which the Defence have had for years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will give its ruling later. Can we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could it be given an ID number for the moment, then, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber has just been informed that the witness may require the assistance of an official from the Victims and Witnesses Unit for purposes of making the solemn declaration. That's why we have her here. So can the witness make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your assistance. Who is examining the witness? Mr. Pisarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Pisarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Petric.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you all right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You feel all right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Super.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even before you came here, we discussed the way in which your testimony would take place. So please, in line with what we said, could you please speak slowly? Could you pause? If there is anything that's not clear to you, please ask again, just make sure that I know about it.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please now state before this honourable Trial Chamber your name and surname?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Andrija Petric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 13th of July, 1962.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you were born?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I was born in a village called Gornji Hasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This village of Gornji Hasic, is it in the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of school have you completed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I have completed a school for telephone operators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a special school?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a special school for disabled persons only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what do you do now?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I am a telephone operator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I'm an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live or rather since when have you been living in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I've been living in Bosanski Samac since 1984.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you live in Bosanski Samac until the present day?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Until the present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am married, and I have two children, and there is my wife, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the hostilities broke out, that is to say the 17th of April, 1992, were you employed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I was employed at the municipal assembly of Samac all the way up to 1992, until the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you spend the entire war in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, the entire time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the conflict broke out, on the territory of Bosanski Samac, the municipality of Bosanski Samac, did you know about the existence of the 4th Detachment of the Yugoslav People's Army in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how come you became aware of the fact that the 4th Detachment of the Yugoslav People's Army existed in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment was not a secret, because all citizens were represented on this detachment, Muslims, Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps learn of this fact through the media?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm just hoping you're not continuing on the 4th Detachment, because -- there is a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It looks like we have some technical difficulties. I will try to resolve this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was some technical problem with the ear phones. I'm sorry, I really didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I was just about to say that I hope you're not continuing with the 4th Detachment. The Trial Chamber feels that it has received sufficient evidence about its existence, unless there is something extraordinary which has not been covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I'm not going to talk about the 4th Detachment at all. I just wished to put one more question in this connection, and I think it has to do with the interests of Mr. Zaric as one of the accused here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in a position to hear Mr. Zaric on radio Samac in a programme together with Radovan Antic and it had to do with the tasks of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I listened to Radio Bosanski Samac and I heard then that the objective of the establishment of the 4th Detachment was only related to the breaking out of a conflict between the citizens of Bosanski Samac. They were calling for peace, tolerance and mutual understanding and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they advocating the prevention of interethnic conflict?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, where were you during the night between the 16th and 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Between the 16th and the 17th, I was in my apartment that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the night, did you hear anything as you were there with your family in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Strong gunfire was heard and afterwards, a few explosions, and then nothing else was heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in your apartment that morning?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I remained in my apartment until the morning. I did not go out anywhere because I had heard from my neighbours that war had started and that people should not go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to work on that day?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Not to work, for reasons related to my personal safety, because I had already heard that the municipal assembly had already been taken by the paramilitary forces, the specials, as we call them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So the building of the municipal assembly where you worked, you heard that it was taken by these paramilitary forces, very well, thank you. Did you hear that a curfew had been imposed in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I heard about that. It was between 10.00 p.m. until the morning so at that time we didn't go out anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you lived in town, did you or any of your friends or neighbours or relatives carry some kind of white ribbons? Were you ordered to wear white ribbons in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I personally did not wear one and I did not observe -- I mean I and none of the members of my family wore a white ribbon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that someone had ordered white ribbons to be worn?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm being told now that something was not entered properly in the transcript. Did you say that you could not observe?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I said I could not observe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, you could not observe. Very well, thank you. At that time, was the town of Bosanski Samac shelled?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Already at that time, frequent shelling started, living conditions in town had already become difficult, there was no power, water, supplies were increasingly difficult, so that was the situation as it was. It was hard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, that is to say from the 17th of April, 1992, and during the course of 1992, were you ever called up for any kind of work obligation?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I was never called up for any work obligation. I was not and none of my family members were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember and could you please tell the Trial Chamber when and where were you arrested by the police?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of May, sometime in the morning, the police came to my door, to the stairwell, since it was locked downstairs my wife went downstairs, she opened the door and they asked, "Is Andrija there?" And I said I was there. They told me or rather he said to me that I should come with him. And when I went downstairs, I asked where are you taking me and what for? But I did not get an answer to that question. He just shrugged his shoulders, just like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't receive an answer and where did they eventually take you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: We walked as far as the department store. There was a lorry waiting there with people who were standing there. I don't know how many people exactly but not too many at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stand there for?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to remember in terms of time but not too long any way. There were about 20 of us. We boarded the lorry and they took us towards Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just pause please for a minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Just a very brief matter if Your Honours please. It would be wise, I think, for Mr. Pisarevic and of assistance to the Chamber for you to understand this witness's evidence for you to be clear on whether he suffered from his disability back in April of 1992. I rather assume he did but it's not entirely clear and I think it's important for you just so that you can understand his evidence and more clearly. So I respectfully suggest that we just very briefly clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. We'll clarify that although I think we've answered that question. He said he completed special training for disabled persons but we'll go back to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Petric please tell us since when have you been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic now that you've reminded us that he actually said so, there is no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they put you on to that lorry and took you where?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: To Crkvina. We arrived there about 20 of us, we got off the bus -- got off the lorry one by one to a place where the police were waiting for us, and they took down our names one by one, and then we, all of us, went to the football pitch in Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's pause a minute to clarify a number of issues. As you were standing outside the department store where the lorry was waiting, did anyone guard you? If so, who?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a policeman there standing with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those people who were taken together with you to Crkvina, what was their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: All of them were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you reached Crkvina, did anyone take your names down?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in Crkvina, they took our names down. I've said that before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it that took your names?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: The police did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there on the football pitch in Crkvina, who was providing security?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I don't know but I know that it was the police who took our names and then we went to the football stadium and we were there. I don't know who exactly was there because I couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. When you came to the stadium, were there people there already?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: When I came to the stadium, I found there many women, children and men but all of them civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay inside the stadium?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I stayed almost until it got dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at dusk?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: The same group, the 20 of us, they called us back to the lorry and we went to Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly you're talking about the same 20 people who had been taken from Samac to Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you then taken to and who took you there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: We were taken back to Samac, to the gym of the secondary school building, and the police again were waiting for us there, taking our names again, and they stripped us of everything we had, any sharp objects. We had to leave it there and then we went to the hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the gym of the secondary school you're talking about, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the gym, and we were the first group who got in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived there, and when the policemen took your shoe laces, any sharp objects you had on you, did you find any one there already in that gym?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: No, no. There was no one. We were the first group to get in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were the first to get in?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then? Did you remain there on your own or did other people start arriving?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: The following day or two days later, I can't remember, but many people started coming in, and after a while, the gym was full of people. It was really crowded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, if you know, where were those people coming from, the people who were being brought into the gym of the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Those were people from Zasavica itself, Gornji and Donji Hasici, from Samac itself, and I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know those people?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Some of them, I did know, yes. Quite a number of them actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I stayed for 11 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stayed for 11 days in the gym of the secondary school in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this is a convenient time for a break, and then we can continue later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will continue at 1250 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Petric, can we proceed, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During the 11 days you spent in the gym of the secondary school, did your wife or any of your family try to have you released?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes. My wife went to the municipal assembly because I used to work there, to try to have me released through those people there, and she went to the SUP as well but to no avail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This means she went to the police. Do you know who she spoke to there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Probably Mr. Stiv.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say Stiv --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I mean Stiv Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. While you were there, did your wife manage to bring you food, clean underwear, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: My wife tried, not every day, but almost every day, and almost every day she managed to bring some food, although we only received food there once a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone maltreat you personally in any way while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: No, no one abused or maltreated me but they were maltreating some other people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that some other people were maltreated, can you say who it was that maltreated the prisoners there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: For the most part, people in camouflage uniforms would come barging in, specials as we called them. Personally I was never beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, what happened on the 11th or rather 12th day of your stay there? Did anyone call your name out?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: On that day, on the 26th of May, about, I believe, 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning, people came whether from the police or one of the guards, because they were all police for me, and they called out about a hundred names and asked us to stay in the hallway of the secondary school building. They told us that we had to make our choice, because the International Red Cross would soon be there and we should tell them whether we wished to be exchanged or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. When your name was called out, when you came to the hallway, you were no longer in the gym?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The police or rather the policemen who called out the names, did you have an opportunity to meet or to talk to the representatives of the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: All of us who were lined up in the hall, we went one by one, and the others remained, some sat down and spoke softly. It was done on an individual basis. There was a translator helping us translating our statements. Personally I said that I did not wish to be exchanged because I had my wife back at home and a small child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us, please, this person from the International Red Cross, was it a man or a woman?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I think it was a lady and the translator was a man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So you told them you did not wish to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about all the remaining 99 persons who were there? Did they also say whether they wished to go or not to the representatives of the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of them, and after about half an hour, those of us whose names had been called out, all hundred of us, there were two lorries waiting outside and we boarded the two lorries, all of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you boarded those lorries and where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: To a village called Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. When you came to the village of Zasavica, what happened there? Where did you stop? Were you still in those lorries? What did they explain to you as to what the procedure would be for the exchange?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: The lorries pulled over. We got off the lorries. They called out our first and last names and they told us that as soon as there was a group of six people, that we should go six by six in groups of six, to the boat, because that was the only way it could be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You refer to the boat now. What this means, if I understand you correctly is that the exchange was supposed to take place across the river?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, across the River Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was your name called out too as part of this group of six people for the exchange?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was called out too. There were six of us at one point we were standing about 20 metres from the lorry, I saw a group of people who were standing there, and I recognised Simo Zaric's voice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us pause a minute here. How many people were in that group? And could you tell if they were civilians or some other people?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many people were there. I was quite agitated. I can't remember how many people were there at that moment but I do think they were civilians. I approached Simo then because I had recognised his voice and I told him that I did not wish to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you told Mr. Zaric that you did not wish to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Zaric tell you then?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: He told me: Andrija, at this moment there is no way for me to help you. Because I came myself to meet my family from Trnjak and Dubica coming this way. The only thing I can do for you is to tell you that I didn't know that they could return with the International Red Cross and that I should say the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So while you were in the lorry, when you set out towards the River Bosna, you didn't know that on the river bank where the exchange was taking place, there were representatives of the International Red Cross present too?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know. No one informed me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard Mr. Zaric's voice. You approached him and spoke to him and Mr. Zaric told you that there was nothing he could do to help you, but he advised you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he told you that on the river bank of the River Bosna there were representatives of the International Red Cross and that you should speak to them about help, ask them to help you and tell them that you did not wish to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you continued on with the group towards the River Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were six of us. We reached the river bank, and that's when I saw people in white coats. I walked up to them and I asked them whether there was anyone there from the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Did you recognise any of those people wearing white coats on the river bank?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised Mr. Veljo Maslic and they asked me is there was anything you need? And I said that I did not wish to be exchanged and then someone translated this for them and they said what did you say and then it was translated and they said fine they understood what I said so they took me aside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you came there, you recognised Veljo Maslic, you spoke to this group of people there, asking them whether there was anyone there from the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke to them and you told them that you did not wish to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: They wanted to know the reason, and I said again that my wife was back at home, and that we had a small child too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone translating what did you say?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a translator. They understood and they told me I should step aside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person who told you that they had understood that you did not wish to be exchanged, was that a man or a woman?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I can't remember right now, what the gender was of the person there. I was really very excited and I really wanted to go back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were told to --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: To step aside, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that moment, was anyone else told to step aside or were you the first person who left the group or the groups before yours?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I was among the first because I insisted on that. I was adamant. There were other groups of six people, people would pass by and ask me what are you waiting for here and I said well, I'm here because I refused to be exchanged. There were eight other persons who stepped aside from the group and stayed with me where I was standing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those eight persons also said on the spot that they did not wish to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when the exchange was finally completed? Did anyone from the other -- from the opposite side of the River Bosna call upon you to change your minds? Tell us about what happened?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: When the exchange was completed on the other side of the River Bosna, there were nine persons, nine of us, standing there, myself and eight other persons, people were shouting from the other side of the river that we should think twice that we should change our minds, and agree to be exchanged. They shouted over to us and wanted us to stand separately so that they could see us, but to no avail. They were not successful and then the last thing they shouted over to us is "May you all die."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they verbally abusing you or cursing you because you refused to cross to the other side?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I suppose they were shouting in anger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us who was on the other side of the River Bosna, across the River Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: There were Croats, Croats only, standing on the opposite river bank, the two warring sides, one side on one river bank and the other side on the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were Croats leaving from this side of the river. Who was arriving from the other -- from the opposite side, from the opposite river bank, from Odzak?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Arriving from the opposite side, from the direction of Odzak, were Serbs who had been detained in Odzak, in prisons in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the nine persons standing there change their minds? Did anyone finally agree to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: No, no one changed their minds, everyone remained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the exchange was completed, what happened to you next?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: When the exchange was completed, we got back on to the lorry and went back to Samac, to a company, I think the name was Tekstilac. We all got off the lorries there and each of us went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the same lorries that had taken you away brought you back to the Tekstilac factory and after that you all went home, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm positive about myself. I went home. I don't know where the others went but I certainly went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do next when you came home?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: The next day, I went to a village to see my father-in-law. I spent sometime there. Only because of the conditions in Bosanski Samac, the living conditions in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you eventually return to live, to reside in Bosanski Samac, in your flat?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I returned as soon as the situation was a bit more stable, as soon as the conditions in the town improved. That's when I returned. And I am still there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your flat, the one you returned to, where is it? Is it in the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: My flat is plum in the centre of town, in the pedestrian zone, that's how we call it. It was hit by a shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When your flat was hit by a shell, like other flats there, were any of the people living in that building killed on that occasion, in your building?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes. The building was destroyed, the building collapsed, there were casualties. One person was killed and some people were disabled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The transcript says that the whole building collapsed. As far as I understood only some of the floors caved in?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, some of the floors caved in, not the entire building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your flat was so damaged in fact that you could no longer stay inside the flat?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes. The flat was damaged to the extent that I could no longer live there, and I was allocated some overt accommodation, temporary accommodation of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your flat was damaged and you had to speak to the authorities, to the municipal authorities to provide some other accommodation for you. So did you go there and speak to them?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I was awarded temporary accommodation. I obtained a certificate that I could use on a temporary basis a flat that had been abandoned by Ibrahim, I can't remember his last name, but it was only a temporary thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, your time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just another minute, Your Honours, please, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the municipal assembly or rather a body of the municipal assembly issued you with a certificate on temporary accommodation in an abandoned flat?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it was Ibrahim's flat. Wasn't it Ibrahim Salkic, known as Ibela?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you stayed there until when?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Until I managed to mend my flat, to carry out all the reparations and everything and then I returned to my flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You still reside there, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the arrest in May, during your entire stay, did anyone bring you in, arrest you or interview you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: No. I was never again brought in or interviewed or arrested or interrogated by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my examination, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just one question. Cross-examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petric, my name is Pantelic I defend Blagoje Simic before this Tribunal. My learned friend and colleague Pisarevic asked you or rather you told him that you went to see your father-in-law because the living conditions there were better than those in Samac. When you said better living conditions, did you mean to say that the conditions in Samac were poor because there was no electricity, water, because there had been shelling? Is that what you were referring to? Is that why you went to stay temporarily with your father-in-law?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes. The town had been shelled heavily, there was no water, electricity. There was a shortage of supplies, and where I went to, they had some food after all, and there was less risk involved, less risk to personal safety, in terms of shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At your father-in-law's house you felt much safer and the conditions were better, is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, very briefly, just a clarification stemming from the examination-in-chief. Cross-examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Petric?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm Novak Lukic, Defence counsel for Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Pleased to meet you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were born from Donji Hasic, born in Donji Hasic and when you were describing the gym at the school and you said that people were on the next day brought from Gornji Hasic, Donji Hasic et cetera so that they were your people from your village, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about those ten, 11 days while you were in the gym of the school. Do you know whether they took some people out of there to the SUP? Do you know anything about that? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes. The police called out some people's names. Any way, they came and took people out individually. I don't know where. But I just know that they would call out someone's name and then this person would go away and be returned later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution? The Prosecution? MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Petric, my name is Di Fazio, I'm going to ask you a few questions on behalf of the Prosecution. I'll try to be as brief as I can.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The people who initially arrested you at your home, were they local police?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: The people, the police who arrested me at my apartment, I mean I did not know them. I don't know the names of these persons. Well, maybe, but I simply don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did any of them have foreign accents?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear that because they were -- I mean they did not answer any of our questions so I cannot really remember how they spoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So there is nothing that you can tell us as to whether or not these people were locals or otherwise? Or perhaps a combination of locals and people from outside of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's speculation, asking him to speculate whether these were locals or a mixture of locals he said he doesn't know. MR. DI FAZIO: It's not speculation I'm asking him specifically if there was anything that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the question is proper and the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot confirm that because I don't know these people. I did not contact them. I mean it's not that I didn't contact them but whatever I asked, I didn't get any answers so I personally do not know. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now you just briefly mentioned to us just a moment ago in answer to Defence counsel that police came into the high school gym and took away prisoners for questioning. Can you tell us if those police officers were locals or whether they were from elsewhere? Or both?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately again, I cannot since I cannot see properly, I was not in a position to know, because they just called out people's names and surnames and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. I understand that but is there anything perhaps that you heard that might indicate whether or not the police officers who came in to the high school gym and took away prisoners were foreigners?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know how to answer that question really. I think it was the people who guarded us who called out these names, and we were guarded by the police. They were the security there, the guards there, the police was, and I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did -- can you recall any of the names of the local police who came and called out names?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps only one policeman, Predo. I wouldn't know anybody else. But he just guarded us there, our names would usually be called out in the morning, and in the evening, to see whether we were all there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, just if you can answer questions with a yes or a no that would speed up things and hopefully we can finish quickly. In May of 1992, you were a telephone operator?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't possess any weapons?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I never had a weapon. I'm a disabled person. I didn't do any military service, sir, or anything so I never had a firearm, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely. And you weren't a member in May of 1992 or indeed at any time in 1992 of any paramilitary formation or supported any paramilitary formation in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: No, never. I never supported any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Now, you were arrested for no good cause. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I don't know any reason, because when I was taken, I was asked -- I asked why did you arrest me? And I didn't get an answer. I asked a few times and I asked different people, but none of this succeeded. There was just silence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You were never ever provided with an explanation as to why you had been arrested, taken to Crkvina and then placed inside the high school gym by anyone in authority?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: No, no one ever said anything to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, the men who were in custody at the high school gym were all Croats, weren't they? Or in the main Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: All were Croats. That's for sure. At the high school gym.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you and you know, don't you, Mr. Petric, that the only reason you were there along with those other men was the fact that they were Croats? Simply because of your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Well, nobody told me. I asked for them to tell me why I was there, but nothing was confirmed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I heard that and I understand that and I'm not disagreeing with you. What I'm suggesting to you is that you know, don't you, that the only reason that you and all of the other men in the high school gym were imprisoned in that place is because you were Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can't confirm that. That's precisely what I asked them to tell me and that's not what they told me so I cannot confirm that. Had somebody said that to me -- I mean, it's only what I can think but nobody ever said that to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, on the -- in late May, around the 25th of May, at that time, your wife was living in Bosanski Samac, correct? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your children were still in Bosanski Samac, correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had at least your father-in-law living in Bosanski Samac, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: No. He lived in a village which is called Tursinovac near Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. And your wife and you also had other relatives and family living in Bosanski Samac at that time, cousins, aunts, uncles, extended members of your family?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I did but I didn't go anywhere else, for safety reasons only, because of the shells and everything else, I didn't move about much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And at that time, in May of 1992, no one in Croatia was asking for you to be exchanged and taken from Bosanski Samac, were they?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I can't hear this. Oh, yes, now I can hear it. I didn't hear this right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. At the time of your exchange, no one in Croatia, as far as you are aware, was seeking you, was asking for you to be exchanged, taken out of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: No, nobody was looking for me, and I really don't know whether anybody was looking for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's go to the day of your exchange. You had an opportunity to speak to some people whom, as far as you were aware, were members of the International Committee of the Red Cross, and that was in or close to the high school gym and before you were taken off to the exchange point?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: It was precisely in the hallway of the high school. I have already said that we had been lined up in the hall and these people who were sitting were perhaps four or five metres in front so they were a bit further away. So one by one we would walk up to them, speak quietly, and of course she would write that down and that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. However, all I'm interested in is this: The people who you spoke to in the high school, in the hallway, as far as you could tell, were not locals but members of the International Committee of the Red Cross? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: They were members of the Red Cross because they just spoke a foreign language and then this was being translated. I didn't understand what they were saying in their language so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And just if you can answer yes or no, you made it clear to these foreign people who were members of the Red Cross that you did not wish to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What followed from that was that you were taken from a prison, put on a bus, and taken to the river where the exchange was taking place?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the bus was Mr. Miroslav Tadic present?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: It was a truck, not a bus. I did not see him. I can't say that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know him and can you recognise his voice?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: No. I don't recognise his voice. I don't know him really. Perhaps I never spoke to him personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if he was present -- I know you don't know him but did you hear from anyone else, do you have any other information, indicating his presence or otherwise? If you don't know, say so.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At the actual exchange, the people that you spoke to and expressed a desire not to be exchanged were essentially two, Mr. Zaric and the Red Cross, the International Committee of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: No, no. Mr. Zaric was not there. I mean he was there in front of the truck with a few people, and they were talking, that's what I said, whereas the Red Cross was right by the banks of the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But you had an opportunity to speak to the International Committee of the Red Cross and again for a second time make it clear that you did not wish to be exchanged, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was then, in the presence of the International Red Cross at the exchange that you were permitted to remain, not forced to actually cross?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: No. I was not forced to cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What's your father's name?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
utterances.text: My father's name is Djuro. He was also present at that exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any other Andrija Petrics living in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA PETRIC
